title: When quiet reading stops counting as focus
statement: How long a reader may go without interacting before time stops counting as focused is unsettled: real reading looks idle, and the window in use is an unvalidated guess.
example: One reading course stops counting focus 25 seconds after the child's last action, a figure no observed session data set.
detail: A grade-3 reading course's points rubric counts time as focused while the child has done something in the last 25 seconds, and arriving on a page counts as doing something, so quiet reading time counts. The rubric marks the 25 seconds as its own number rather than the live rules': nothing in the live rules fixes it, no observed session data set it, and it is a deliberate guess in the generous direction. An analysis of the points simulation names the trade-off: a child genuinely reading taps nothing for minutes at a time, so a tight window under-counts what a reading course wants to reward, while a loose one over-counts a child who has wandered off.

evidence.quote: The 25s idle window is generous by design and unvalidated by data.
